# Conclusion

## Summary

This project looks at how job satisfaction in Switzerland differs between groups of workers, how it changes around major economic events, and whether the differences between occupations stay the same over time. We use 21 waves of the Swiss Household Panel (2004–2024). After combining and cleaning the annual files, we obtain 305,462 observations from 45,632 people. Since the job-satisfaction question is only asked to people in work, our employed sample contains **124,769 observations from 22,265 individuals**. We first described the data one dimension at a time, then estimated linear regressions (OLS) with standard errors clustered by respondent, because the same people answer the survey in several years. The regressions are unweighted; the survey weights are only used to check the overall trend.

Five findings stand out. **First**, average job satisfaction fell slowly, from 8.212 in 2004 to 7.815 in 2024 on the 0–10 scale, and the decline is slightly larger when the survey weights are used (8.207 to 7.711). **Second**, satisfaction differs between occupations: agricultural workers, managers and professionals are more satisfied than clerical support workers, with gaps between about a quarter and just over half a point. **Third**, age, sex, region of residence and employment arrangement also matter, with age showing the largest differences, but together these characteristics explain only about 4% of the differences between individuals. **Fourth**, the economic events are not followed by the same reaction: satisfaction hardly changes in the 2009 crisis year, is slightly lower around the 2015 franc shock and is temporarily higher in 2020, although part of this increase may come from the new SHP sample that joined that year. **Fifth**, the gaps between occupations change over time (χ²(24) = 45.88, p = 0.0046), with several groups losing ground relative to managers in 2020–2024. These results answer our research questions at a first, descriptive level: workers' characteristics and the period in which they are surveyed are linked to job satisfaction, but our models do not show why. For organisations, the main message is that satisfaction differs between groups, especially by age and occupation, but group averages cannot replace listening to their own employees.

## Limitations

The first limitations concern the **data**. We start in 2004 because the general job-satisfaction question was not asked between 2000 and 2003. We also lose observations along the way: the employed sample only includes people with a valid occupation and satisfaction score, and the adjusted regression keeps 104,526 observations from 18,363 respondents, because every variable in the model must be observed. If the people we drop differ from those we keep, for example if less satisfied workers are more likely to skip questions, our averages could be slightly too high. The people in the panel also change over time, as some leave the survey and new samples join, for example in 2013 and 2020. A change in the yearly average therefore does not always mean that the same people became more or less satisfied. Finally, the region variable describes where people live, not where they work.

There are also limitations in how we **measure and model** satisfaction. Job satisfaction is a personal judgement on a 0–10 scale, and most answers are at the top of the scale, so a linear model is a simplification and very satisfied workers have little room to report further increases (a ceiling effect). Clustering the standard errors takes into account that the same people answer several times, but it does not control for characteristics we do not observe, such as income, personality or working conditions. The regressions also do not use the survey weights or the full design of the SHP: almost all observations have a valid weight, but so far we have used the weights only to check the overall trend. We have not yet run full model diagnostics. The event windows compare survey years, so they cannot show that the 2009 crisis, the 2015 franc shock or COVID-19 caused the changes. Finally, because we test many groups and interactions, a few results could be significant just by chance. Our conclusions therefore apply to the SHP respondents we analysed and should not be generalised to all Swiss workers or to other countries without further checks.

## Future Work

Before the final report, we plan the following steps:

1. **Focus on one economic event.** Following the feedback on our proposal, we will choose one of the three events and study it in more detail. We will compare the same respondents before and after the event and, if the SHP industry variables allow it, workers who were more and less exposed to it, such as export-oriented jobs during the 2015 franc shock. This would help separate the effect of the event from the general downward trend.
2. **Look more closely at selected groups.** We will use the EDA and the occupation × period results to select the groups with the most interesting patterns, such as clerical support workers, workers aged 25–34 and the occupations that lost ground relative to managers in 2020–2024, and follow their satisfaction over time.
3. **Follow the same people over time.** Because new samples join the SHP, for example in 2013 and 2020, we will compare changes within the same individuals, for example with a respondent fixed-effects model, so that the results are not driven by who enters or leaves the panel.
4. **Use the survey weights in the models.** We will repeat the main regressions with the SHP cross-sectional weights and check whether the size and direction of the differences stay similar to the unweighted results.
5. **Check the models and the data definitions.** We will look at the residuals and try alternative age groups and event windows (for example, two years before and after each event). Because satisfaction only takes whole values from 0 to 10, we will compare the results with an ordinal model. We will also check that the employment-arrangement categories are coded the same way in every wave.

These steps build on what we have already done. The aim is not to add many new analyses, but to make the existing results more reliable and to answer the research questions in more depth: starting from the broad picture and then narrowing down, as suggested in the feedback on our proposal.
